A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

The critical distinction is probate. In states with expensive or slow probate processes — California, New York, Florida, and many others — a living trust pays for itself many times over. In states with simplified probate procedures (like Texas or Wisconsin for small estates), the cost advantage of a trust is smaller but the privacy and incapacity benefits still apply.

According to recent reports, you need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

Sources indicate that the term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

Recent findings suggest that an irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:.

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

In a recent development, nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

It has been revealed that the remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

According to recent reports, remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate initiative.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific complications or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

According to recent reports, A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

Sources indicate that A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

Recent findings suggest that the living trust vs will decision is not about which is better — it is about which is better for your specific situation. For estates with more than $100,000 in probatable assets, especially in high-cost probate states, a revocable living trust saves thousands of dollars and months of delay while providing incapacity protection and privacy that a will cannot match. For smaller estates in simplified-probate states, a well-drafted will with proper beneficiary designations may be all you need. Either way, the worst estate blueprint is no estate plan. More than 60% of American adults have neither a will nor a trust, leaving their families to navigate probate without guidance, pay avoidable costs, and endure unnecessary delays during the most difficult time of their lives.

Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that betMGM paid MGM $34 million in distributions and brand license fees in the third quarter, while MGM's Las Vegas Strip earnings fell 12%. The online venture's profit rose 112%, but its iGaming growth trailed a slowing US market.

According to recent reports, MGM Resorts’ third-quarter 2026 results, released October 28, revealed its online partner becoming a source of cash as Las Vegas softened. MGM now receives both distributions and brand license fees from the venture. On the Strip, lower room rates hurt results.

According to recent reports, betMGM sent $68 million in total to its two owners, Entain and MGM, during the quarter. That sum combined $18 million in parent fees and $50 million in cash distributions. A year earlier, MGM had expected the payments to begin in the fourth quarter of 2025, with an initial payment of at least $100 million.

According to recent reports, betMGM’s net revenue rose 7% to $710 million from $667 million. iGaming accounted for $483 million of that, up 6%. Online sports net revenue reached $216 million, up 7%. Profit grew faster than revenue, with nine-month adjusted EBITDA reaching $185 million.

Industry observers note that betMGM holds 14% of gross gaming revenue across its active markets, including 20% in iGaming and 8% in online sports betting. It kept its 2026 guidance of $2.9 billion to $3.1 billion in net revenue and $300 million to $350 million in adjusted EBITDA. However, it now expects results near the bottom of both ranges.

Its 6% iGaming gain lagged the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, the slowest rate on record, according to Citizens JMP Securities. Growth had been 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. State results varied, with growth of 7% in Pennsylvania, 10% in Latest Jersey and 17% in Michigan.

In a recent development, regional Operations revenue fell on a reported basis to $883.2 million from $956.9 million. The drop reflects the April 2026 sale of MGM Northfield Park’s operations for $546 million. Removing $83.7 million from sold properties leaves a prior-year same-store base of $873.2 million. Measured against that base, the regional business grew slightly.

Recent findings suggest that MGM Digital, which includes LeoVegas but not BetMGM, grew revenue to $184 million from $174 million. Its segment adjusted EBITDAR loss narrowed to $4 million from $23 million. CEO Bill Hornbuckle said MGM’s digital businesses delivered strong revenue growth.

According to recent reports, taken together, the figures are consistent with digital operations offsetting part of the weakness on the Strip. The next test for the online market comes from DraftKings, which reports third-quarter results after the market closes on Thursday, November 5. Its conference call follows on Friday, November 6, at 8:30 a.m. ET.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eagles running back Saquon Barkley sold his equity stake in Polymarket after NFL rules barred players from holding prediction-market investments. The case sets the league apart from the NBA and MLB, which have signed deals with the exchanges, as the NFL argues at the Supreme Court that sports event contracts are gambling.

Industry observers note that saquon Barkley no longer owns a piece of Polymarket. The Eagles running back sold his equity stake to comply with league rules, he told Front Office Sports in an interview published October 28. It is the first public case of the NFL applying its gambling rules to a player’s prediction-market investment.

Barkley bought into Polymarket before the league told players they could not hold such investments. The NFL goes over endorsement, investment and training rules with players before every season.

According to recent reports, the league has now made clear that its sportsbook restrictions extend to prediction markets. It declined to comment on Barkley’s case specifically. The stance was not fresh to players. Kalshi and Polymarket were already off-limits to them as endorsers or brand ambassadors in January 2026. At that point, prediction markets were treated as gambling entities under the league’s gambling policy.

In a recent development, the NFL’s approach puts it at odds with other major leagues. Polymarket became Major League Baseball’s Official Prediction Market Exchange on March 19, 2026. On October 26, 2026, the NBA named both companies its preferred prediction-market exchanges. The agreement gives them rights to league intellectual property and marketing.

Industry observers note that NBA players face far lighter limits. They can hold stakes in the exchanges and appear in their marketing. The line is drawn only at promoting contracts on NBA games.

Recent findings suggest that the split also shuts NFL players out of an industry that leans heavily on their sport. By the league’s own figures, football made up $1.8 billion of prediction-market trading on the season’s first Sunday. That was more than half of the day’s total.

Industry observers note that the league is pressing that view at the Supreme Court. On October 8, 2026, it filed an amicus brief supporting Newly introduced Jersey’s request for review in Flaherty v. KalshiEX, case No. 26-299. The NFL argued that sports prediction contracts are gambling. In its view, they are not financial swaps under exclusive federal oversight.

New Jersey filed its petition on September 2, 2026. It followed an April ruling in which the Third Circuit sided 2-1 with Kalshi. The appeals court found that the CFTC has exclusive oversight of sports-event contracts.

Exclusive: Saquon Barkley tells FOS he was forced to divest his equity stake in Polymarket.

NFL players are not allowed to invest in or endorse gambling or prediction market companies.

— Front Office Sports (@FOS) October 28, 2026.

Many of the NFL’s concerns will be addressed through the CFTC’s ongoing rulemaking, Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana stated. In her view, the agency already has the power to police sports-related event contracts.

The Supreme Court granted Kalshi a 30-day extension to answer Upcoming Jersey. Its response, originally due October 8, must now be filed by November 9.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A federal judge has barred Illinois from licensing, taxing or prosecuting sports event contracts listed on CFTC-regulated exchanges.

  • The order reaches three state tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal judge has barred Illinois from licensing, taxing or prosecuting sports event contracts listed on CFTC-regulated exchanges. The state's appeal sends the fight to the Seventh Circuit, which already has prediction-market cases from Wisconsin.

It has been revealed that illinois has lost, for now, its power to police sports event contracts traded on federally regulated exchanges. Judge Martha Pacold’s order in the Northern District of Illinois turns her early-October ruling into a formal injunction. It covers contracts listed on CFTC-regulated platforms such as Kalshi and Coinbase.

The order reaches three state tools. They are the Sports Wagering Act, the criminal gambling statute and an Illinois Gaming Board internet-wagering rule. The budget’s prediction-market fees fall with the licensing rules, because they apply only to providers holding a state license. Her first ruling had left the tax question open and called for more argument on the fees.

The stakes are significant. Fiscal 2026 was the first year of the state’s per-wager tax on licensed sports wagering.

Sources indicate that the Gaming Board had already tried to act. It sent cease-and-desist letters to KalshiEX, Crypto.com and Robinhood on April 1, 2025. Polymarket received one on Jan. 27, 2026. Those letters cited the Sports Wagering Act (230 ILCS 45) and the criminal code (720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)).

According to recent reports, lawmakers then took a different route. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the budget containing the new framework on June 16. Under the package, which includes SB 3019, prediction markets became exchange wagers under the Sports Wagering Act and needed a Gaming Board license. Each transaction carried a tax that would climb once a licensee passed five million exchange wagers. In September, Republican Rep. Travis Weaver filed House Bill 5811 to repeal the exchange-wager tax. His bill would leave the licensing rules in place.

In a recent development, licensed online and mobile sportsbooks face their own costs. A first license for that category costs $15 million and runs four years, with each four-year renewal priced at $1 million.

Courts are divided on whether state gambling laws reach CFTC-regulated sports contracts. Pacold’s order is a rare win for Kalshi and the federal regulator. Before her early-October decision, Kalshi had lost 16 federal court rulings in a row. In that opinion, Pacold found the state’s other laws in conflict with federal law because they control “what can be sold, as well as where it can be sold and to whom.”.

Sources indicate that the CFTC sued Arizona, Connecticut and Illinois on April 2, 2026, over their actions against federally registered designated contract markets. Chairman Michael Selig stated the agency would defend market participants against “overzealous state regulators.”.

There are now 5 prediction-market appeals before the Seventh Circuit involving sports-event contracts:.

According to recent reports, · CFTC v. Wisconsin· Kalshi v. Raoul· Coinbase v. Raoul· United States v. Illinois· Ho-Chunk Nation v. Kalshi https://t.co/NH7qLf591x.

— Daniel Wallach (@WALLACHLEGAL) October 31, 2026.

It has been revealed that for operators, the injunction offers room to keep listing sports contracts in Illinois for now. For the state, it removes a revenue stream and an enforcement path at once. Anticipating a legal challenge, legislators had kept the tax’s revenue out of their budget projections. The outcome now depends on a single appeals court.

Recent findings suggest that on July 29, Judge William Griesbach ruled against the CFTC in Wisconsin, and the agency took that case to the Chicago-based court. Illinois has asked the Seventh Circuit to reverse and vacate Pacold’s order.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The most highly anticipated video game of the decade is here.
  • It has been revealed that in a statement shared with Wccftech, the technical team at Rockstar has confirmed that GTA VI uses different upscaling solutions across all consoles in order to achieve a balance between visual quality and performance with a target of 30FPS.
  • As for rendered resolutions, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and PlayStation 5 Pro all start with a native base resolution of 1440p, which is then upscaled to 4K.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The most highly anticipated video game of the decade is here. GTA VI arrives almost 13 years after GTA V, with reports suggesting that it has already generated around $1.54 billion in revenue from 16 million preorders. Ahead of its release, Rockstar Games has finally shared some technical details, including rendering resolutions and upscaling technologies being used across all consoles.

It has been revealed that in a statement shared with Wccftech, the technical team at Rockstar has confirmed that GTA VI uses different upscaling solutions across all consoles in order to achieve a balance between visual quality and performance with a target of 30FPS. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use Rockstar's own temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) solution, while the PlayStation 5 Pro relies on Sony's second-generation PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR2). The Xbox Series S, meanwhile, relies on AMD's FSR 4 upscaling technology.

As for rendered resolutions, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and PlayStation 5 Pro all start with a native base resolution of 1440p, which is then upscaled to 4K. The Xbox Series S is the least powerful console; thus, the game runs at a lower base resolution of 720p, which is upscaled to 1080p using FSR 4. The final image on all consoles is then composited with a 4K user interface before being presented.

Rockstar has also developed a physically-based material library for GTA VI and a cinematic imaging pipeline to deliver realistic lighting, reflections, and material details within the game. The team claims it has worked to maintain a consistent lighting solution across all consoles, including the Xbox Series S, while adjusting ray-traced global illumination (RTGI) features depending on each platform's hardware capabilities.

In a recent development, the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S rolled out all the way back in 2020, and while the consoles have capable hardware, their architectures are finally beginning to show their age. The fact that Rockstar is targeting just 30FPS across all consoles, while relying on different upscaling technologies and rendering resolutions, highlights how much performance is potentially being left on the table in order to maintain visual fidelity. That being mentioned, a PC release of GTA VI continues to be a major question mark. Rockstar is yet to announce a release date or even provide a launch window, meaning that PC gamers can only rely on Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream the game on their systems.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, nvidia’s GeForce driver 621.14 is reportedly causing excessive background writes on idle PCs, inducing extra wear on SSDs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the bug is described by user Andergraude in an Nvidia forum post as “fresh in 621.14,” which came out on Nov.
  • It has been revealed that the “real writes” point comes from the fact that a per-process write counter is not the same as writes reaching the drive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, nvidia’s GeForce driver 621.14 is reportedly causing excessive background writes on idle PCs, inducing extra wear on SSDs. One user measured about 3GB an hour on the susceptible driver, and another mentioned estimated up to 30GB/hour on the newer 621.24. This follows a similar-looking bug from AMD’s video driver discovered last month.

Recent findings suggest that the bug is described by user Andergraude in an Nvidia forum post as “fresh in 621.14,” which came out on Nov. 4, who says it operates by “continuously [rewriting] the binary log file” with “real writes” to the drive. The writes are coming from the NVDisplay.Container.exe process, or the “NVIDIA Display Container LS” service, which logs to the nvlog.nvlgstg file. This background service is necessary for running the Nvidia Control Panel and App. It’s not clear what’s written in the log, and not every system is necessarily impacted.

It has been revealed that the “real writes” point comes from the fact that a per-process write counter is not the same as writes reaching the drive. The measurements came from Windows Resource Monitor, Windows performance counters, and CrystalDiskInfo. The Data Units Written counter matched Windows’ reporting. This test indicated 515MB of process I/O coming with 270MB of total writes to the C: drive over five minutes. That works out to roughly 3GB per hour, in line with the user’s own estimate.

In a recent development, worse, “the write volume increases as the file grows.” Stopping the service and deleting the log can temporarily reduce the writes. With the previous driver version 621.01, the writes totaled less than 2MB per five minutes, and a second user in the thread confirmed that a rollback helps.

According to recent reports, mitigation attempts, such as three clean reinstalls with the help of DDU from that second user, did not fix the problem. The writing process also impacted gaming and video performance, potentially causing hitching, which suggests it gets worse under load.

Another user, AyzekUorren, in a separate thread about driver 621.24, which came out Nov. 12, states that it could get up to “about 30gb per 1h” or even “70gb or even more” with longer sessions. This is even with telemetry disabled in the Nvidia App. Noted is that every Alt+Tab added 500MB to 1GB of writes, at least for this user.

In AMD’s case, it was the External Events Utility, or atieclxx.exe, that exhibited constant writes on an idle PC. In that case, the AMD utility was reportedly copying its own executable every second. To put the impact into context, the AMD bug had rates reported between 0.3 and 5MB/s while total drive writes in the 621.14 test measured around 0.9MB/s.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, the Nvidia numbers are somewhat alarming, given that a typical 1TB SSD is rated for 600TB of writes over a standard five-year warranty. Even at 270MB per five minutes, this could be about 28TB per year — for a never-sleeping PC — which is reaching toward 5% of the drive’s rated endurance, although the writes include everything the system is writing and realistic uptime will be less. However, at the higher end — 30GB per hour, at eight hours a day — one could see 15% of drive endurance worn every year for nothing.

This doesn’t make it a drive killer, but given how much consumers value drive endurance, especially with SSD prices as they are, avoiding unnecessary writes like this is certainly a priority. To see if you’re affected, check Resource Monitor and look for the telltale NVDisplay.Container.exe and the nvlog.nvlgstg file in the list. You can also check the SMART Data Units Written value with CrystalDiskInfo or equivalent, such as your drive’s SSD toolbox.

Recent findings suggest that at this time, no fix or hotfix has been announced, and the best workaround is to do a rollback. A similar matter in the past, fixed with driver patch 471.96 back in 2021, was covered by Nvidia’s release notes. As it stands, Nvidia has “N/A” for 621.24’s Open Concerns, and the company has not acknowledged the bug. For the AMD bug, the driver wasn't fixed for over three weeks (and came as an optional update).

AMD Japan's X account has been met with sharp reproach after claiming the firm loves gamers and values its interactions with gamers above all else, with commenters and even a community note expressing dissent at the sentiment, owing to AMD's comments on its "data center-first" ethos and a commitment to AI that has driven the price of consumer PC gaming up to nearly unaffordable levels.

Quoting a Tom's Hardware post on the X social network discussing CEO Dr. Lisa Su meeting gamers and autographing a GPU, the AMD Japan account was quick to seize the moment. "AMD values its interactions with gamers above all else," the post read, but it was met with a stark reminder that gamers don't feel the same way. The post soon received a newly introduced community note that pointed out that AMD's own CEO doesn't agree. In fact, Su was quoted as saying that AMD is now "a data center-first company," with the note also pointing to the fact that AMD's data center revenue increased 97% year-over-year, as per its Q3 2026 earnings report. That equates to around $8.5 billion in revenue, while client and gaming revenue fell 8% to $3.7 billion. Gaming alone was down 40%.

At the time, Su remarked that AMD expected its server revenue to double year over year in 2027, with its data center AI revenue growing at an even faster rate. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth," the CEO said during the organization's earnings call.

By comparison, the same call heard Su say that, in 2027, AMD was "planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage." With this all in mind, it's perhaps no surprise that the AMD Japan X account stirred such a strong response from gamers who feel that AMD has left them behind in search of a more lucrative data center market. AMD is certainly not alone in that regard. Nvidia, once the darling of the PC component enthusiast, is now focused on AI data center components instead. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today's best RAM will look huge compared to upcoming DDR6 memory.
  • According to recent reports, JEDEC's DDR6 preview highlights improvements in various areas, including performance, capacity, reliability, and power efficiency.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the most notable differences is that DDR6 memory modules will measure just 74mm in length, 44% shorter than DDR5’s 133mm memory modules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today's best RAM will look huge compared to upcoming DDR6 memory. JEDEC has just released a preview of the DDR6 specification, confirming that next-generation memory modules will be 44% shorter than DDR5. That is only the physical aspect, though. From a performance perspective, DDR6 will debut at 12.8 GT/s, more than double DDR5's baseline transfer rate, while also quadrupling the memory bandwidth per memory module thanks to a fresh design.

According to recent reports, JEDEC's DDR6 preview highlights improvements in various areas, including performance, capacity, reliability, and power efficiency. These advancements align with the upgrades DDR5 brought to the table when it launched.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most notable differences is that DDR6 memory modules will measure just 74mm in length, 44% shorter than DDR5’s 133mm memory modules. This makes DDR6 only 6% longer than DDR5 SO-DIMM modules, which you commonly find in laptops and mini-PCs.

JEDEC has maintained the pin count for many years, sticking to 288 pins for DDR4 and DDR5. However, DDR6 may finally break that mould. Given the substantial reduction in length with DDR6 and the data bus width upgrade, it is reasonable to assume that DDR6 will have a completely different pinout and density. Sadly, JEDEC has not revealed the pin count for DDR6.

It has been revealed that early rumors suggested that DDR6 may be limited to CAMM form factors to feed the AI boom. However, JEDEC's announcement at least does not rule out other form factors. It appears JEDEC is still determining which form factors DDR6 will use. Potential options include RDIMM, UDIMM, and CAMM formats, just like DDR5.

Baseline JEDEC Transfer Rates (MT/s).

Baseline JEDEC Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s).

Peak JEDEC Transfer Rates (MT/s).

Peak Baseline Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s).

Notably, JEDEC has increased the data bus width in DDR6 to 96 bits, a 50% boost over DDR5's 64 bits. The channel architecture for DDR6 will also change substantially. While DDR4 and DDR5 leveraged a single 64-bit channel and two 32-bit sub-channels, DDR6 takes a different approach. JEDEC will implement a design with four 24-bit sub-channels.

Using the baseline for comparison, DDR6 offers up to 153.6 GB/s of total module bandwidth, compared to DDR5's 38.4 GB/s. That is a 4X uplift in bandwidth. If we compare DDR5-9200 RDIMMs, which max out at 73.6 GB/s per module, with DDR6-12800 RDIMMs, the uplift is a little more than double.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

At least on the server side, DDR6 RDIMMs will start at DDR6-12800, whereas DDR5 RDIMMs topped out at DDR5-9200. JEDEC anticipates DDR6 reaching DDR6-14400 and beyond. This is for the server and enterprise market, though. It remains to be seen which DDR6 speed will launch in the consumer market. DDR5 commenced at DDR5-4800.

Sources indicate that DDR6 may be shorter than DDR5, but it makes up for it by having 2X the bank count. This will help push higher data rates and capacities. DDR6 will support 128Gb (16GB) dies, which represents a massive leap. We are looking at 4X the density of early DDR5 memory modules. Instead of placing chips side by side on the PCB, DDR6 enables die stacking, allowing manufacturers to place multiple dies on top of each other via Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs).

In a recent development, consumer DDR5 memory modules right now sit at 64GB per module, while server RDIMMs have reached 512GB. DDR6 could raise module capacity to 128GB or 256GB and potentially scale RDIMMs to 1TB or more per slot.

DDR6 has no official launch date. Many believe 2029 is a realistic target for commercialization. However, in the current state of things, it would be a miracle if DDR6 had no setbacks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the flaw was dubbed Java4Shell by Calif Research, the lab that found the vulnerability.
  • You can see an exploit of the bug in action below across multiple software services.
  • According to recent reports, the actual bug is a flaw in an optimization for Base64 decoding, functionality that's ubiquitous in any programming language.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the flaw was dubbed Java4Shell by Calif Research, the lab that found the vulnerability. The researchers say it rates 9.2 on the newer CVSS 4.0 scale, though individual reports from companies like Oracle itself and Red Hat give it their own ratings, but they're all in the 8 to 9.8 range depending on the vendor. The root cause is a bug in OpenJDK, the library that nearly every distribution of Java, whether Oracle's or anyone else's, derives their implementations from.

You can see an exploit of the bug in action below across multiple software services.

According to recent reports, the actual bug is a flaw in an optimization for Base64 decoding, functionality that's ubiquitous in any programming language. Base64 is a format to allow for easy transformation of binary data into plain text. In the modern day, it's used to embed files in the middle of text, like inserting image data in the middle of HTML or CSS, attaching files to emails (internally they're all text-based), or simply representing data as text for visual inspection, like file checksums or cryptographic key fingerprints.

Oracle has already fixed the bug and issued updated versions of its wares. However, much like digital certificates, operating systems and even individual programs include their own copy of a Java executable, meaning that the potential blast radius is far wider than you'd expect at first glance. Calif listed many such common applications: at the time of the post, Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and PingFederate all had full unauthenticated RCE, while Apache Kafka Broker, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker have RCEs after authentication.

Sources indicate that because Java is so darn widespread, most every company has to matter security advisories and updates for their wares, including IBM, Red Hat, Siemens, and Broadcom. Because so many containers also use Java-based applications in some form, those too are vulnerable, and the count of individual vulnerable container images across registries everywhere is likely a high figure. This is likely not a bug that will be easily eradicated.

Recent findings suggest that there is a condition to trigger the exploit, but it's not too difficult to fulfill. The Java instance in question must be running on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 support and the VBMI extension. In practice, that means chips from the Intel Ice Lake and AMD Zen 4 families, from 2021 and 2022 respectively, for their server variants. Older CPUs are not affected, as the code optimization that contains the bug is specific to VBMI.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that the specific bug is in a hand-written assembly optimization that fails a simple bounds check. If an attacker inputs 64 As and an "=" sign as padding, they can overwrite neighboring memory, and then weaponize that corruption, similar to how Heartbleed worked. As usual these days, Calif says that the vulnerability was found by an AI bot, with $200 worth of tokens. Though unlike many other examples, this one was actually fairly deep, and it wasn't low-hanging fruit that illustrated poor code or network security hygiene.

Three 'e-waste' Nvidia V100s hit 100 tokens per second on Qwen 3.6 35B in a $1,042 homelab rig

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A homelab builder benchmarked three used Nvidia V100s on Qwen 3.6 35B, achieving about 100 tokens per second in a custom setup costing $1,042 with just “e-waste” GPUs.
  • The blog post, “Scaling ‘E-Waste’: LLMs on Multiple Decommissioned GPUs,” compares nine different builds — one to three K80s, P100s, or V100-16GB cards — on a single Supermicro dual-Xeon board.
  • “E-waste,” in this case, refers to decommissioned enterprise GPUs, which are a popular but somewhat underpowered option when compared to very expensive modern alternatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A homelab builder benchmarked three used Nvidia V100s on Qwen 3.6 35B, achieving about 100 tokens per second in a custom setup costing $1,042 with just “e-waste” GPUs. The smaller, dense Qwen 3.6 27B manages about 24 tokens per second on the same platform, and the V100s use about half the energy of the same number of P100s for a given job.

The blog post, “Scaling ‘E-Waste’: LLMs on Multiple Decommissioned GPUs,” compares nine different builds — one to three K80s, P100s, or V100-16GB cards — on a single Supermicro dual-Xeon board. The test uses llama.cpp and covers more than 130 LLM tests, including Qwen 2.5, Gemma 4, and, of course, Qwen 3.6, at Q4/Q8/F16 precisions and from 4K to 128K context sizes. GPU energy per run is also recorded. The builder is “daily driving Qwen 3.6 35B” on the V100s and notes that scaling decommissioned GPUs will only get you so far.

“E-waste,” in this case, refers to decommissioned enterprise GPUs, which are a popular but somewhat underpowered option when compared to very expensive modern alternatives. The Nvidia Tesla V100s in question are tested as a follow-up to a July round which tested 15 “e-waste” GPUs, and this time the board and CPUs stay the same for every build — the Supermicro X10DRG-Q with two Intel Xeon E5-2687W 12-core CPUs, powered by the Corsair HX1500i PSU.

It has been revealed that performance is judged based on what is considered “realtime interaction” which, here, is 70 tokens per second. As to why the number of GPUs is three: Qwen 3.6 35B, the primary tested model, fails on just one or two at Q8, or 8-bit quantization.

Here are the given prices, with the note that they aren’t “100% reflective of what you could find on eBay today,” although the totals count only one of the two CPUs and omit RAM, storage, the case, and any cooling.

The older cards are relatively inexpensive because they “run hot and ship without cooling,” which required the builder to 3D print one blower duct per card and has led to the development of a standalone cooler.

Industry observers note that the bench itself involves 10 runs of 512 generated tokens per test with context pre-filled to 4K, 32K, 64K, or 128K. Qwen 3.6 35B is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, which only activates about 3 billion out of its 35 billion total parameters per token. The numbers that immediately follow are at Q8.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The token goal was easily reached…when the context window was small, or 4K. The 100.8 tokens per second there fell to 72.7 at 128K, still usable by the 70 tokens per second goal. The 27B model, which is not MoE, fared much worse, at 24.3 at 4K, 21.6 at 32K, 18.7 at 64K, and just 14.2 at 128K. The MoE ends up about four to five times faster, depending on the context size.

It has been revealed that also tested were other dense models of about 30B parameters. At 4K, Gemma 4 31B achieved 20.9 and Qwen 2.5 32B 21.0, while the MoE Gemma 4 26B cleared the 70 tokens per second bar with just two V100s at Q8. If you move down to Q4, or 4-bit quantization, two V100s can run Qwen 3.6 35B at 77.1 to 105.4 tokens per second, between 128K and 4K context size. This is where it’s claimed that adding more cards gives you more memory, which enables larger models to be run, but not speed.

The P100s, for comparison, only hit 40.2–55.2 tokens per second in the same context range with Q8 Qwen 3.6 35B, and the target 70 only with Qwen 2.5 3B. If we compare to more modern hardware — the Nvidia DGX Spark, MSRP $4,700, and the M5 Max Mac Studio, which starts at $2,499 but costs $5,399 with the tested 40-core GPU, 128GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD — the 3x V100 build holds its own, using sourced data.

The Mac comparison comes from the oMLX benchmark page for the M5 Max with 40 GPU cores and 128GB of unified memory, and that hits 43.9 tokens per second with a ~195K-token prompt on the Qwen 3.6 35B model. The Mac is slightly ahead at 4K and 32K, while the V100s pull ahead at 64K and 128K, by 19% at the longest context. These numbers have to be taken loosely, as the machines use different runtimes.

Recent findings suggest that the Spark run came from Kleybrink’s dgx-spark-bench, using Ollama in thinking mode with short prompts. Its 45.8 tokens per second is less than half the V100s’ 4K figure.

Going further to modern GPUs, which “destroy our decommissioned equivalents,” as the builder puts it, you get about 315 tokens per second on two H100s and about 455 on one B200 at 128K, the B200 roughly six times the V100 box, even though the hosted cards ran the full 16-bit model against the V100s’ 8-bit. Parasail, an inference provider, sponsored that comparison with dedicated H100 and B200 deployments.

Recent findings suggest that as for energy, the V100 setup came out to about 0.02 kWh for a 128K 35B run, with the P100s taking twice that much and two or three K80s as much as 0.35 to 0.45 kWh. The V100-16GB simply “[puts] up better scores while consuming less energy,” in comparison to the P100s. These numbers are for the GPUs and not from the wall.

There’s more to come. The builder wants a benchmark that “maps to ‘software factory’ performance,” a term for models being prompted constantly, around the clock, where instant speed matters less. Then there’s the cooler, which is “almost ready for release,” with beta testers to be recruited from the mailing list, although no date has been given. From the Reddit thread, the builder mentions the intention to compare inference backends and use speculative decoding to improve performance.

Ukraine deploys homemade 'flying modems' in daring drone attack to destroy Crimean Bridge, ditching Elon Musk's Starlink

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ukrainian forces ditched Elon Musk's Starlink wireless system and used their own relay network of "flying modems" to maintain a live feed of an attack on the Crimean Bridge, even amid Russian attempts to block the signal.
  • Industry observers note that videos of the attack showed Flamingo missiles, carrying a 1,200kg warhead, being remotely piloted towards the bridge.
  • With Starlink, or Starshield, no longer fit for Ukraine's needs, it turned to the "flying drones" instead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ukrainian forces ditched Elon Musk's Starlink wireless system and used their own relay network of "flying modems" to maintain a live feed of an attack on the Crimean Bridge, even amid Russian attempts to block the signal. The attack, which led to the partial collapse of the bridge, was significant for a number of reasons. The bridge is one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most symbolic assets due to its linking of the occupied Crimean Peninsula and Russia. But perhaps more importantly, the attack's use of Ukrainian connectivity technology highlights the country's lessening of its reliance on Starlink. The modems were crucial to the success of the mission, with the FT reporting that they kept missiles connected to their pilots while they manoeuvred through Russia's air defenses.

Industry observers note that videos of the attack showed Flamingo missiles, carrying a 1,200kg warhead, being remotely piloted towards the bridge. Flamingo missiles are capable of traveling at around 590 miles per hour, requiring a stable and reliable video feed. It's reported that the Ukrainians deliberately chose not to use Starshield, the military version of Musk's Starlink, for the operation, with the firm's satellite network having been restricted in recent weeks. That restricted service would have been insufficient for the Crimean Bridge attack, forcing Ukrainian forces to find another solution. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that he has not been told why Starlink's connection has been throttled, with neither the White House nor the Pentagon being forthcoming. SpaceX, Starlink's parent company, has also so far not provided any explanation. However, relations between Zelenskyy and Musk appear to be strained, with the SpaceX CEO saying that Ukraine had "gone too far" by striking Russian data centers.

With Starlink, or Starshield, no longer fit for Ukraine's needs, it turned to the "flying drones" instead. The flying communications towers were used as a relay, boosting the signal sent from individual missiles so that it could more readily reach their pilots. This approach allowed the weapons to fly farther while still maintaining a reliable connection, allowing them to bypass Russian air defense systems and attempts to block their signals in the process. Without the relays, Ukrainian drone pilots have previously had to program missiles with coordinates and then rely on their autopilot system. They were inevitably shot down because they could not be steered away from Russian defenses.

Perhaps ironically, Ukraine isn't the first country to use flying communications towers. Russian forces were using similar technology as early as 2023, before the system began using a Chinese mesh networking system.

Intel Diamond Rapids reveals signs of life in SC26 demo running live server

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly.
  • In a recent development, the demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller.
  • In a recent development, of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly. Most interesting was a running server at the CXL booth, showcasing a demo with a Diamond Rapids CPU. The server ran for the first day of the show, and upon returning to the booth, we were informed that it had been shut down due to noise complaints (it’s hard to mistake a running server). Elsewhere at Bull’s booth, a Diamond Rapids CPU was shown installed in a server behind a glass case. Notably, Intel didn’t have a Diamond Rapids demo, instead focusing most of its booth on Xeon 6+ and its new D270 GPU, otherwise known as Crescent Island.

In a recent development, the demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller. If you’re unfamiliar, memory expansion via CXL is an increasingly common tactic to give multi-host environments access to a large pool of memory, breaking free of an individual server’s capacity via CXL. In the demo, Montage is showing off its memory expansion controller running across a Xeon 6 and a Diamond Rapids server, each sharing a pool of memory over CXL. CXL is an open standard, built atop PCIe.

In a recent development, of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild. The 256 GB memory capacity shown doesn’t provide any hints, either. Intel has unveiled that Diamond Rapids will support 16-channel memory, with RDIMM support up to 8,000 MT/s and MRDIMM support up to 12,800 MT/s, matching AMD’s recent EPYC Venice CPUs. However, Intel hasn’t revealed capacity, though we anticipate the maximum capacity will be far above 256 GB – for context, last-gen Granite Rapids-AP supports up to 3 TB per socket.

Bull is a French server designer focused on HPC and AI infrastructure, and it demonstrated off two Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids chips installed in the Bullsquana XH31600 server. As expected for a 2P Diamond Rapids server, it supports 32 channels of DDR5 memory, and it’s designed for a liquid-cooled deployment.

In a recent development, as you can see from the image, these aren’t production chips. They’re labeled with “Intel confidential,” and the code starts with “Q,” revealing that this is a sample. Originally, we expected to see Diamond Rapids in the second half of this year, perhaps around this time. However, in August, Intel revealed that Xeon 7 chips would launch in 2027.

Based on the various servers we saw and the live demo, it seems Intel is targeting a launch earlier in the year, likely in Q2; we expect a larger consumer focus in Q1. It could slip later into the year, though that seems very unlikely given that Diamond Rapids was already pushed back, and the insatiable demand for CPUs in AI data centers doesn’t appear to be drying up.

Industry observers note that also pointing to a relatively quick release are the various servers we saw on the floor at SC26. Several partners showed off their next-gen servers built for Diamond Rapids CPU, sporting the LGA 9324 socket, including Dell and Asus (pictured above). However, Bull was the only vendor we could find that had an actual chip on display.

Diamond Rapids is Intel’s true next-gen CPU, following up on the E-core-only Xeon 6+ range that launched earlier this year. Diamond Rapids packs up to 256 P-cores, and it’s built on Intel’s performance-enhanced 18A-P node. The most interesting aspect of the chip is its topology, with Intel breaking from its previous layout and building something much similar to an EPYC CPU. The package features centralized memory and I/O, which were pushed out to the edges of the package with Granite Rapids. You can read more about the design of the chip in our Diamond Rapids recap from Hot Chips on Tom’s Hardware Premium.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

Silicon Motion demos SM8466 PCIe 6.0 SSD controller, expected to ship by 2028 — controller boasts improved quality of service, samples imminent

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that silicon Motion is showing off its PCIe 6.0 SSD controller for data center applications for the first time at the SC26 conference in Chicago.
  • Silicon Motion introduced its high-end MonTitan SM8466 enterprise SSD controller designed for next-generation data center and hyperscale storage applications at FMS 2025.
  • To improve performance and reduce latency, Silicon Motion has developed its Separate Command Architecture (SCA), which separates command and address transmission paths within the NAND interface to improve parallelism and increase effective throughput.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that silicon Motion is showing off its PCIe 6.0 SSD controller for data center applications for the first time at the SC26 conference in Chicago. The final iteration of Silicon Motion's SM8466 controller was taped out recently, and drives based on the chip are due in late 2027 or early 2028. However, the upcoming controller also has a secret weapon designed to ensure consistent performance of SSDs under concurrent workloads that may set it apart from competitors.

Silicon Motion introduced its high-end MonTitan SM8466 enterprise SSD controller designed for next-generation data center and hyperscale storage applications at FMS 2025. The controller features a PCIe 6.x x4 host interface and 16 NAND channels to enable sequential transfer speeds of up to 28 GB/s, random performance of up to 7 million 4K IOPS, and capacities of up to 512 TB and beyond as newer 3D NAND devices emerge. Just like other high-end data center-grade SSD controllers released in recent years, the SM8466 complies with NVMe 2.0 and OCP NVMe 2.5 SSD specifications.

To improve performance and reduce latency, Silicon Motion has developed its Separate Command Architecture (SCA), which separates command and address transmission paths within the NAND interface to improve parallelism and increase effective throughput. Additionally, the controller supports Silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology, which enables programmable performance limits and predictable quality of service (QoS) across concurrent workloads, which is arguably its most vital differentiator against rivals who rely on different methods of guaranteeing performance.

It has been revealed that in addition to its performance chops, the MonTitan SM8466 incorporates advanced error correction, virtualization, data protection, and security features. The controller's error correction engine supports low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with 4KiB codewords and Silicon Motion's 16KiB Collaborative Codeword (CoCo) technology to improve data integrity and reliability with advanced NAND flash memory. The controller also supports Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV), MPF virtualization, SMART diagnostics, and comprehensive data protection mechanisms. Security capabilities include Secure Boot, AES-256 encryption, TCG Opal compatibility, and firmware attestation. Together, these features make the SM8466 suitable for high-capacity data center drives that are expected to deliver high performance, predictable latency, and reliable operation under demanding data center workloads.

Silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology builds upon the original PerformaShape architecture introduced with the tech giant's PCIe 5.0-based MonTitan SM8366 enterprise SSD controller several years ago. The 1st Generation implementation uses dedicated hardware accelerators and two-stage leaky-bucket regulators to control read and write performance in terms of IOPS and throughput, both for individual workloads and for the SSD as a whole. This approach enables data center operators to prevent one workload from monopolizing SSD resources at the expense of others.

PerformaShape 2 retains these capabilities but doubles the number of supported quality-of-service (QoS) sets from 256 to 512 and introduces more sophisticated performance controls to accommodate a larger number of concurrent workloads with different requirements. One of the key additions to PerformaShape 2 is Multi-Dimensional Shaping, which enables the controller to coordinate performance limits across multiple I/O characteristics rather than enforce each limit independently. This gives data center operators greater flexibility when allocating SSD resources among applications with different performance requirements.

Another key enhancement of PerformaShape 2 is support for NVMe TP4176, a proposed extension to the NVMe specification that aims to standardize performance management and QoS controls. Whereas the original PerformaShape relies on Silicon Motion's vendor-specific NVMe commands and a dedicated host driver, TP4176 could eventually enable compatible host software to configure performance policies through a standardized mechanism. The technology is particularly relevant for cloud environments where SSDs serve numerous virtual machines, containers, and applications whose storage requirements can change considerably over time, according to the firm.

Recent findings suggest that pakistan's telecommunications authority, the PTA, has confirmed that internet connectivity issues affecting the country's residents are related to the failure of an international submarine cable. SEA-ME-WE 5 is located almost seven miles off the coast of Pakistan, near the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz, and connects the region with European networks via the Middle East. The TWA notes that the outage may have caused intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality, with Transworld Associates (TWA) working to identify the cause of the issue. The outage comes weeks after the Islamic Republic of Iran described several undersea fiber cables that run through the Strait of Hormuz as "legitimate latest targets" in the ongoing tensions in the area. February's start of military action by the United States, Israel, and others has made the Strait of Hormuz a household name in recent months. General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, pointed out that as many as seven "large cables pass beneath the Strait of Hormuz, and all internet and commercial data pass through them," going on to say they are "legitimate" targets for the group.

Sources indicate that one of the international submarine cable systems, the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5), have reported a fault at about 11 KM from Pakistan shore which may cause some internet users to experience intermittent connectivity complications and a decline in service quality. Transworld Associates (TWA) is coordinating with the SMW5 Consortium to identify the root cause of the fault and determine the Estimated Time for Restoration (ETTR). In the meantime, internet traffic is being rerouted through alternative international links to minimise the impact and ensure service continuity to the greatest extent possible. #SMW5 #SubmarineCableFault #InternetDisruption #InternetUpdate #PakistanInternet #ConnectivityUpdate #InternetServices #DigitalPakistan #PTA #TransworldAssociates #TelecomUpdate #NetworkRestoration #StayConnected #InternetConnectivityNovember 18, 2026.

Notably, the SEA-ME-WE 5 cable does run through the Strait of Hormuz, although it should be stressed that there is at the moment no indication that this outage was caused by any act of sabotage. However, that is no doubt something that the TWA investigation will seek to confirm before it can apply whatever fix is necessary to fully restore services for those in the region.

Sources indicate that undersea cables are vital for maintaining connectivity between nations and continents, and Iran isn't the only one to have taken note. A Russian ship was chased from British waters by a Royal Navy attack helicopter earlier this year after it was found less than a mile from five undersea cables. The ship was in the area for 14 hours, and the cables it was near happened to connect the UK with Spain, Portugal, Canada, and the United States.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, said on Thursday that yields of chips made using the company's latest 18A (1.8nm-class) fabrication process have achieved 70%, which is more or less in line with what one would expect from an all-fresh manufacturing technology at this stage of its ramp.
  • "When I took over [as CEO in March, 2025], 18A yield was horrible; now we are at 70%," Lip-Bu Tan noted at the TomorrowX conference (via @firesidealpha).
  • According to recent reports, lip-Bu Tan did not specify whether he meant functional yield, parametric yield, or percentage of sellable silicon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, said on Thursday that yields of chips made using the company's latest 18A (1.8nm-class) fabrication process have achieved 70%, which is more or less in line with what one would expect from an all-fresh manufacturing technology at this stage of its ramp. In addition, Intel and Microsoft have signed an agreement under which Microsoft will secure Intel Xeon supply capacity for years to come and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for in-house silicon.

"When I took over [as CEO in March, 2025], 18A yield was horrible; now we are at 70%," Lip-Bu Tan noted at the TomorrowX conference (via @firesidealpha).

According to recent reports, lip-Bu Tan did not specify whether he meant functional yield, parametric yield, or percentage of sellable silicon. However, it is reasonable to expect a CEO of a semiconductor company to talk about functional die yield, the percentage of dies that pass basic electrical and functional testing.

Intel began volume production of compute tiles of its Core Ultra 300-series CPUs codenamed Panther Lake using 18A in the second half of 2025, so a 70% functional yield seems decent at this stage of the product ramp, though for Intel's economics a lot depends on parametric yield and how many advanced SKUs of Core Ultra 300-series 'Panther Lake' processors Intel can supply to customers at a premium. The same applies to Intel's Xeon 6+ Clearwater Forest processors with up to 288 cores that are in high-volume production now and which use 18A-based compute chiplets along with Foveros Direct 3D stacking.

In addition to announcing an notable 18A milestone, Intel also signed a long-term agreement with Microsoft, under which the latter will secure multi-year Intel Xeon supply capacity, including supply of next-generation Xeon processors codenamed Diamond Rapids, and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for multi-chiplet data center solutions developed in-house.

The EMIB agreement is arguably the biggest news. Microsoft is the first company to publicly commit to Intel's advanced packaging technology for its own silicon (i.e., it does not mean that Microsoft is the first third party to use EMIB; it is the first party to confirm usage of EMIB), which represents a significant commercial development for Intel Foundry in terms of publicity. However, the announcement does not identify the processors involved, their manufacturing process, production volumes, or deployment schedule. Microsoft was the first company to commit to use Intel's 18A for its data center silicon in 2024, though it is unclear whether the newly announced EMIB packaging agreement relates to the same solution or not. As the majority of high-end data center solutions tend to use multi-chiplet design, it is reasonable to expect Microsoft's future solutions for data centers to use EMIB for multi-die processors.

"Through use of our advanced packaging capabilities with EMIB to scale future generations of Azure infrastructure, Intel and Microsoft can combine the flexibility of heterogeneous integration with the manufacturing scale required for the AI era — giving customers upcoming levels of performance and economics when interacting with Azure," remarked Naga Chandrasekaran, EVP, Chief Technology and Operations Officer and General Manager of Intel Foundry.

The Xeon agreement provides Intel with greater visibility into future server CPU demand. Importantly, Microsoft has committed to using Intel's next-generation Xeon 'Diamond Rapids,' although the announcement does not disclose purchase volumes or financial terms.

The collaboration extends beyond processor procurement and EMIB. Specifically, Intel and Microsoft are jointly developing infrastructure capabilities that encompass processor architecture, heterogeneous integration, CXL memory expansion, QuickAssist Technology (QAT) acceleration, and Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) security.

  • In a recent development, liberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a massive leap.
  • According to recent reports, this still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s a newly introduced vibe-coded OS in town going by the name of LiberNT. Its name provides a big clue to its nature: Liber (free), NT (New Technology architecture, as in Windows NT). As it has been released under GNU’s GPL3.0 license, LiberNT also provides a free new way to run apps designed for Microsoft’s Windows 11.

In a recent development, liberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a massive leap. Reading the intro, you might have wondered if this work had a ReactOS connection, and indeed there is. But what started as a fork of ReactOS has already got a newly introduced boot loader, graphics stack, memory manager – and yesterday a new kernel. “LiberNT is not affiliated with or endorsed by the ReactOS project or Microsoft,” insist the devs behind this OS.

According to recent reports, this still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64. Ambitiously, the goal is to develop this OS to deliver a free Windows alternative that is “stable, reliable and efficient.” On that latter point, yesterday’s blog enhancement relays some impressive efficiency and performance stats.

In a recent development, the LiberNT team has benchmarked their eponymous OS against Microsoft’s Windows NT, and it beats it hands-down in 112 of 132 system tests. The testing assessed performance in the following areas: file caching, memory handling, threads and locks, plus FAT32 and NTFS storage. Interestingly, both the free and commercial OS were benchmarked on a Mac with an Apple M3 Pro chip. We scanned through the results, and the worst loss for LiberNT was a 28% performance deficit vs Win11, but it claims some astounding relative performance wins showing the free OS being over 2000% faster.

It has been revealed that the devs are entirely clear about the fact that the operating system was vibe coded. “AI is part of how LiberNT is built. It helps us review and write code, and everything it writes is then reviewed by a human,” explains a section of the GitHub page for the project. “Before anything reaches the main branch, a person runs and validates the end-to-end tests. We care about this project too much to let a regression slip through.”.

Industry observers note that if the above highlights about this latest OS's scope, mission, compatibility, and performance have whetted your appetite, there is the full code available via the GitHub link (top), and even some ready-made builds as bootable disk images. Indeed, I’m quite eager to give this new OS a spin. Hopefully, it works as well as the ambitious developers suggest, and I won’t be disappointed by any stability complications using my daily productivity apps like Firefox, Word, and an old release of Photoshop.

Industry observers note that officers responded to a report of a theft in progress at the Dodgeville Walmart Supercenter shortly after 11:15 a.m. local time on November 19. They pulled over a black Tesla with Florida plates and said a search turned up 125 packages of 30th Celebration boosters.

Police also recovered 112 packages of One Piece trading cards, 26 Pokemon anniversary tin sets, and a Rayquaza Lego set, along with other merchandise still in its packaging.

Police stated the Tesla had traveled to several locations in Wisconsin and Minnesota, as well as Missouri. The department is asking other agencies to come forward if they can link any of the additional merchandise to thefts in their area.

In a separate case in September, an Ohio collector was sentenced to 90 days of GPS monitoring after putting a tracker on a van used to deliver Pokemon cards to Walmart.

Industry News: Nebraska voters appear to reject online sports betting despite nearly $22.5 million campaign

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Both linked measures to legalize mobile wagering through Nebraska's racetrack casinos trailed in unofficial returns.
  • It has been revealed that nebraska voters appear to have turned down online sports betting.
  • A loss would be a rare setback for the industry at the ballot box.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Both linked measures to legalize mobile wagering through Nebraska's racetrack casinos trailed in unofficial returns. A defeat would close off a upcoming market for sportsbooks and shows that doubts about tax relief can beat a heavily funded campaign.

It has been revealed that nebraska voters appear to have turned down online sports betting. Initiatives 440 and 441 would have amended the state constitution and statutes to allow mobile wagering through the state’s licensed racetrack casinos. The Secretary of State’s unofficial count, with 885 of 1,322 precincts fully reporting, had 440 trailing by about 296,000 to 354,000. The companion measure, 441, trailed by about 299,000 to 351,000. The results are not yet certified.

A loss would be a rare setback for the industry at the ballot box. Betting would stay in-person only at Nebraska’s five racetrack casinos. FanDuel, DraftKings and the racetrack operators would not gain a upcoming market. Initiative sponsor Jordan McGrain called the midnight results “pretty clear.”.

In a recent development, tax relief was the core of the pitch. Supporters projected more than $166 million for the state’s property tax credit fund over ten years. Opponents countered that the money would flow to out-of-state gambling companies. Nebraska currently taxes casino gaming revenue at 20 percent. Of that tax, 70 percent goes to property tax relief credits.

In a recent development, A report commissioned by Tax Relief Nebraska, the committee behind the measures, estimated just under $87 million in newly introduced state tax revenue over five years. That projection did not carry the vote. Joey Spellerberg, the state treasurer, backed the opposition and stated voters saw the promised tax benefits as negligible.

Should the unofficial result stand, gambling-harm arguments and doubts about tax relief would have carried a heavily outspent opposition to victory. That is a warning for future online casino and sports betting pushes in other states. It also comes as lawmakers are already restricting sweepstakes and prediction markets.

Sources indicate that the ballot route followed repeated failures in the Legislature. Lawmakers did not send a similar constitutional amendment to voters, including in 2024 and 2025. Tax Relief Nebraska then submitted more than 201,000 signatures for the amendment in late June 2026. It filed 146,000 for the companion statute. Election officials flagged possibly fraudulent signatures collected during the drive.

Funding also drew scrutiny. FanDuel and MGM subsidiary Roar Digital gave more than $3.5 million combined to Tax Relief Nebraska. The Legal Accountability Center asked the state’s disclosure commission to investigate. It cited the companies’ ownership in Ireland and the UK.

The proposed market was tightly drawn. Each racetrack gaming operator could have offered wagering through at most two online platforms. Wagering servers would have had to be located in Nebraska. State regulators would have had until June 1, 2027, to adopt rules for online wagering.

According to recent reports, the count now moves toward certification. County abstracts of votes must reach the Secretary of State by November 23. State canvassers meet on November 30, 2026, at 11:30 a.m. to certify the results. Recounts in eligible races start December 2 at 9 a.m.

The fast-food giant has unveiled a latest limited-time feature that allows customers to upgrade eligible orders with Fritos Flamin’ Hot chips, adding an extra layer of spice and crunch.

Sources indicate that however, there are some restrictions. Crunchy tacos, the Cheesy Gordita Crunch, a la carte Nacho Fries, beverages, and desserts are excluded from the promotion.

  • The latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech.
  • The latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the company's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough. The company has reportedly initiated another round of layoffs, this time across its global information technology (IT) organization, as its chief executive continues to reduce expenses and simplify the company's operations, reports Business Insider.

The latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech. Some employees claim that the reductions could affect a double-digit percentage of the department's workforce of around 2,607 people at 55 sites in 53 countries, so we are talking about at least 260 people if we are talking about a 10% reduction, or as much as 520 if we are talking about a 20% reduction. One has to keep in mind that these estimates have not been independently verified. Intel has neither confirmed the number of affected employees nor identified the specific teams involved. Instead, the manufacturer reiterated to Business Insider that it regularly reviews its workforce to ensure that personnel and financial resources correspond to its strategic priorities.

The latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026. In July, Intel eliminated positions in its Data Center and AI Group. Between July and October, the company submitted nine Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) notices in California, which covered 222 employees, according to Business Insider. The most recent notice, filed on October 22, concerned 67 permanent job cuts at Intel's Folsom campus (which mostly specializes in R&D, hardware validation, and software development), effective October 31. As of November 17, no additional WARN notices had been reported.

Sources indicate that intel employed 81,100 people as of September 27, 2026, including 76,500 employees at Intel itself and another 4,600 at Mobileye and other subsidiaries. This compares with 85,100 employees at the end of 2025 and 108,900 a year earlier, which means that the organization's workforce declined by 4,000 since December, 2025, and 27,800 since December, 2024. respectively.

Intel's workforce reductions began well before Lip-Bu Tan became chief executive in 2025. In 2024, his predecessor Pat Gelsinger announced prepares to eliminate more than 15,000 positions, or approximately 15% of the manufacturer’s workforce. Tan has continued to reduce expenses, eliminate management layers, and discontinue lower-priority projects as Intel attempts to cut costs and reduce losses/improve profitability.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voters in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties each rejected inland casino gambling by double digits on November 3.
  • It has been revealed that with the measure defeated, the license created by House Enrolled Act 1038 cannot be granted by the Indiana Gaming Commission.
  • Sources indicate that allen County, where developers were seeking to build, carried the most weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voters in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties each rejected inland casino gambling by double digits on November 3. The single latest license in House Enrolled Act 1038, tied to a project of at least $500 million, now has no county that can host it.

It has been revealed that with the measure defeated, the license created by House Enrolled Act 1038 cannot be granted by the Indiana Gaming Commission. A repeat ballot is also off the table. State law bars a second public question in any county that voted the measure down.

Sources indicate that allen County, where developers were seeking to build, carried the most weight. The county’s election-night summary counted 102,935 votes on the question, with 40.44% in favor. In DeKalb County, 7,374 voters said no. Steuben County recorded 6,234 no votes.

The stakes were substantial. That minimum investment had to cover both the casino and its non-gambling amenities. At least 60% of that had to be spent within two years of the award. The license also carried a $150 million fee to the state, with $50 million of it going to a fund for former host communities hurt by casino closures.

Recent findings suggest that the projected public return was large as well. A study done for the Indiana Gaming Commission estimated that an Allen County casino could generate $204 million in revenue alongside its annual state tax payments. Under the act, 10% of the casino’s tax payments would have gone to the northeast Indiana regional development authority.

According to recent reports, the process hinged on the vote from the start. The commission’s July guidance stated it would take applications only for a county or counties where voters approved inland casino gambling. None did.

Recent findings suggest that gaming Commission officials stated that with no county passing the referendum, nothing happens, and that any next steps are up to the legislature. That puts operators back in front of lawmakers.

It has been revealed that lawmakers have already redrawn this map once. Instead of creating a upcoming license, a January 22, 2026 committee version of House Bill 1038 would have relocated the Ohio County riverboat license. That inland casino could have gone to Allen, DeKalb, Steuben or Wayne County. The enacted version instead created one new license and eliminated one unused racino license. Indianapolis was kept off the list because a casino there would pull business from the existing casinos in Shelbyville and Anderson.

DeKalb and Steuben counties have turned away a casino in referendum votes. Allen County is still counting but 'no' is leading. https://t.co/rwMo6sIYZ2.

— Niki Kelly (@nkellyIN) November 4, 2026.

According to recent reports, the vote also lands in a state that is narrowing gambling elsewhere. House Bill 1052 lets the commission fine any operator or individual $100,000 for knowingly running an internet sweepstakes game in Indiana, starting July 1, 2026. Peer-to-peer skill-based poker is exempt. Indiana still has no legal online casinos.

Indiana was not alone on Election Day, as Nebraska voters also turned down a gambling expansion. In northeast Indiana, the act’s December 1, 2026 deadline for inland casino license applications now arrives with the commission taking no applications.
