Industry News: 22 leadership insights on ensuring accountability without instilling fear

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix.
  • Accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix.
  • Sources indicate that we asked members of the Fast Company Impact Council how they ensure accountability without creating fear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix. The term can come with negative connotations: If something goes wrong, it means whoever is accountable is to blame. Fearing accountability, some team members may hesitate to take roles that require much of it. Even if they step up, fear can keep them from doing their best work or taking needed risks. We asked members of the Fast Company Impact Council how they ensure accountability without creating fear. Below, 22 of them share their best advice on keeping accountability as a necessary and positive role instead of something people dread. 1. TREAT MISSES AS INFORMATION Be as clear about expectations up front as you are about results afterward. Fear comes from ambiguity: People don’t know what success looks like until they’ve missed it. I set clear owners and outcomes at the start, then treat misses as information. What did we learn, and what do we change? I also name my own misses out loud, before anyone else’s. When the leader models it, accountability stops feeling like judgment and becomes a shared standard the whole team owns. — Megan Noel, Covista 2. MODEL SELF-REFLECTION Accountability is less likely to create fear when leaders hold themselves accountable to the same standards and deadlines they expect of others, are honest about where they fell short, and share the lessons they learned. The more leaders model that kind of self-reflection, the more comfortable others will feel doing the same—and helping their teammates build that skill. — Grace Keith Rodriguez, Caliber Corporate Advisers 3. FOCUS ON LESSONS LEARNED Accountability should give people the confidence to take big swings. When it only indicates up for the misses and mistakes, you create a culture of fear, which doesn’t inspire creativity or big thinking. Instead, be clear about expectations, set ambitious goals together, and when something falls short, focus on the lesson learned and move on. — Max Friedman, Givebutter 4. LEAD WITH CURIOSITY RATHER THAN BLAME Accountability without fear begins with clarity—clear expectations and realistic goals—balanced with my personal commitment to being accessible and providing timely feedback. This shared accountability builds trust as the same standards apply at both levels. When challenges arise, I am able to lead with curiosity rather than blame, asking “What happened, and what support do you need?” which creates space for my team to surface issues early and treat setbacks as learning opportunities. Consistency reinforces this sense of safety, so instead of fearing accountability, my team feels supported and invested in our shared success. — Maurice Twomey, Roto 5. ENSURE REAL ALIGNMENT FROM THE START Many tend to think of accountability as something you create at the end of a process. Someone didn’t do what they were supposed to do. Will you hold them accountable or not? In my experience, however, accountability issues are often alignment issues in disguise. What are we trying to do and why? By when? What are we both assuming? What is really feasible? Good leaders ensure there is real alignment around these questions at the start of a process. They approach accountability not as a punishment question but as a clarity question—and in doing so, they debunk the idea that accountability and fear must come hand-in-hand. — Maril MacDonald, Gagen MacDonald 6. OWN THE OUTDATED DASHBOARD Accountability isn’t perfection. A team member flagged outdated targets on a dashboard I was presenting. I owned it and thanked them. Small moments like that set the tone for the big ones. When we miss a real target, we own our work and our choices and solve it as a team. Do that consistently, and you build that muscle for the harder moments. — Michele Walsh, UNICEF USA 7. SHIFT THE MINDSET When leaders shift their mindset from “don’t break this” to “let’s try this,” accountability becomes about outcomes and learning. As leaders, we need to role model what strong accountability looks like and acknowledge fear with grace and empathy. This means we should understand that some good ideas won’t stick, and we should celebrate innovative thinking even when it doesn’t result in a win. When people see their leader take a smart risk, own what follows, and adapt promptly, they do the same. — Jacqui Canney, ServiceNow 8. CUT THE ENDLESS APPROVAL CHAINS If you want real accountability, let team members own the outcome and cut the endless approval chains. Nobody likes to fail, but you can build a culture of permissible failure and actually walk the talk. When mistakes happen, address them head-on, take the lesson, and move on fast. — Khozema Shipchandler, Twilio 9. ASK WHAT HAPPENED, NOT WHO DID IT Make the destination crystal clear and the path flexible. Fear shows up when people don’t know what “good” looks like until they miss it. I’d rather over-communicate the outcome, agree on ownership out loud, and let people choose how they get there. When something goes sideways, my first question is “What happened?” not “Who did this?” Accountability is a promise teammates make to each other, not a punishment waiting to happen. — Colby Proffitt, Seekr 10. MAKE ACCOUNTABILITY A WEEKLY RHYTHM Accountability works when colleagues do the flagging, not the leader. Every week, especially in our executive meetings, we review our trackers top to bottom and call out anything blocked or at risk, in the open, in front of the team. It’s rare that someone gets blindsided in a one-on-one weeks later. Fear creeps in when accountability feels personal or arbitrary. A visible, weekly rhythm makes it structural instead, and that is what keeps people honest without making them defensive. Consistent communication is key. Beyond email and Slack, good ole phone calls and texts are quite effective. — Cody Barbo, Trust & Will 11. TEACH CLEAN ESCALATION For our team, it all starts with providing clear communication so people understand what’s expected and how success will be measured. We approach conversations from a point of kindness and empathy, which includes listening and practicing radical candor so everyone is provided honest, respectful feedback and knows where they stand. Teaching clean escalation and other techniques also plays a role in maximizing accountability while preserving the best possible team dynamics. When people know they can raise issues early and get help addressing them, taking responsibility becomes much easier. — Leerom Segal, Klick Health 12. DON’T LEAVE PEOPLE GUESSING Clarity, transparency, and continuous communication. That is the foundation—and frankly, it is the ethos on which we built our company. When people know exactly what is expected, where they stand, and that honest feedback flows early and often, there is nothing to fear. Fear creeps in when people are left guessing. The goal is shared accountability. Not imposed from the top down but owned collectively by a team that feels genuinely empowered. When that culture exists, people hold each other to a higher standard because they want to—not because they have to. — Meredith Rosenberg, NU Advisory Partners 13. THE KIND OF FEAR MATTERS Fear isn’t always bad. Fearing your boss is different from fearing you didn’t do your best work. Top-down fear can produce compliance, but rarely excellence. I want my team accountable to themselves first, because people only do their best work on things they care about. That means clear quarterly and annual goals, professional development funds for growth areas, honest conversations about where they want to go, and a real grasp of why our work matters and why their contribution is key. People who hold themselves to a standard outperform people who only answer to a boss. — Muneer Panjwani, Engage for Good | The Halo Awards 14. ATTACH A HUMAN OWNER TO AI-RELATED DECISIONS I would argue that it is the lack of accountability that creates fear. Accountability should remove ambiguity. Each artificial intelligence-related decision should have a human owner. There are clear rules of engagement that establish what is and is not in the bounds of permissibility. And when mistakes are made, they are inspected and not concealed. Fear breeds in darkness: Create light. — Scott Brighton, Bonterra 15. HAVE EMPLOYEES SET THE BAR FOR THEMSELVES Accountability is a matter of doing what you commit to. Our team members have some flexibility to set expectations regarding the timing and scope of their deliveries. Publicly demonstrating finished products in team or client meetings improves accountability. Fear is effectively removed when trying to clear bars we set for ourselves. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps 16. SHOW VULNERABILITY Model that it’s ok to own up to a mistake. We’re only human and no one is perfect. Ultimately that leads to greater accountability because there is an honesty at the heart of it. It removes the bullshit and gives folks the support they need to own their accomplishments, warts and all. — Helen Andrews, Johannes Leonardo 17. SET CLEAR EXPECTATIONS Every employee plays a role in the company’s overall success, but depending on their level or access to senior leadership, they may not see how their contributions impact the greater whole. What is crucial to the CEO? What are the growth ambitions of the company? How does each individual’s responsibilities ladder up to the organization’s goals? It is essential to set clear expectations for each person, provide honest feedback, and communicate transparently about how daily activities and individual performance are linked to company success. — Celia Jones, FINN Partners 18. WRITE IT DOWN Accountability holds when the measure is agreed before the work starts. Clarity is kindness, as they say. Set it together, write it down, and review it on a fixed schedule so a missed target shows up early and gets treated as information. People get defensive when the standard appears after the result, or when it shifts depending on who’s asking. Other than that, I try to give real guidelines and real feedback. If you start off that way, it instills the proper expectation of communication. — James Chester, WVN 19. DISCUSS HOW TO CLOSE THE PERFORMANCE-EXPECTATION GAP I try to set a high bar of excellence by sharing great work, and by praising and rewarding excellent work. That way, when someone isn’t delivering, we can point to the gap between their performance and the expectation and talk about how to close the gap. It’s designed to create a supportive, safe, and fair environment. No finger pointing and passive-aggressiveness allowed! — Phillip Haid, Public Inc. 20. TAKE AN ASPIRATIONAL APPROACH I’ve learned that empathy and accountability aren’t opposites. A few years ago, I leaned too far into being accommodating, and expectations slipped. I used to frame performance gaps as “We’re not where we need to be,” which I think created fear. Through coaching, I learned to take a more aspirational approach: “This is what excellence looks like. How can we get there?” It shifts the focus from fear to problem-solving. When people care deeply about the mission and understand what’s expected of them, accountability becomes a shared responsibility rather than something driven by fear. — Felicia Curcuru, Binti 21. REPLACE PUNITIVE REACTIONS WITH CURIOSITY AND COLLABORATION Having experienced the damage of fear-based leadership early in my career, I know criticism and punishment only breed toxicity and burnout. Accountability without fear starts with connecting our work to purpose. At a mission-based organization, holding ourselves accountable is directly tied to achieving our mission. When performance issues arise, leaders should replace punitive reactions with curiosity and collaboration. Approaching staff with two-way dialogue to uncover blockers, rather than one-way scrutiny, turns accountability into a partnership that helps everyone succeed. — Jaymes Black, The Trevor Project 22. SEPARATE THE PERSON FROM THE OUTCOME Accountability works best when expectations are clear before something goes wrong. I try to separate the person from the outcome, so the conversation becomes about what happened, what we learned, and what needs to change. Fear makes people hide problems. Clarity makes them easier to solve. — George Kailas, Prospero.ai.

Accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix. The term can come with negative connotations: If something goes wrong, it means whoever is accountable is to blame. Fearing accountability, some team members may hesitate to take roles that require much of it. Even if they step up, fear can keep them from doing their best work or taking needed risks.

Sources indicate that we asked members of the Fast Company Impact Council how they ensure accountability without creating fear. Below, 22 of them share their best advice on keeping accountability as a necessary and positive role instead of something people dread.

Recent findings suggest that be as clear about expectations up front as you are about results afterward. Fear comes from ambiguity: People don’t know what success looks like until they’ve missed it. I set clear owners and outcomes at the start, then treat misses as information. What did we learn, and what do we change? I also name my own misses out loud, before anyone else’s. When the leader models it, accountability stops feeling like judgment and becomes a shared standard the whole team owns. — Megan Noel, Covista.

Accountability is less likely to create fear when leaders hold themselves accountable to the same standards and deadlines they expect of others, are honest about where they fell short, and share the lessons they learned. The more leaders model that kind of self-reflection, the more comfortable others will feel doing the same—and helping their teammates build that skill. — Grace Keith Rodriguez, Caliber Corporate Advisers.

Recent findings suggest that accountability should give people the confidence to take significant swings. When it only shows up for the misses and mistakes, you create a culture of fear, which doesn’t inspire creativity or big thinking. Instead, be clear about expectations, set ambitious goals together, and when something falls short, focus on the lesson learned and move on. — Max Friedman, Givebutter.

Industry observers note that accountability without fear begins with clarity—clear expectations and realistic goals—balanced with my personal commitment to being accessible and providing timely feedback. This shared accountability builds trust as the same standards apply at both levels. When challenges arise, I am able to lead with curiosity rather than blame, asking “What happened, and what support do you need?” which creates space for my team to surface concerns early and treat setbacks as learning opportunities. Many tend to think of accountability as something you create at the end of a process. Someone didn’t do what they were supposed to do. Will you hold them accountable or not? Good leaders ensure there is real alignment around these questions at the start of a process. They approach accountability not as a punishment question but as a clarity question—and in doing so, they debunk the idea that accountability and fear must come hand-in-hand. — Maril MacDonald, Gagen MacDonald.

When people see their leader take a smart risk, own what follows, and adapt rapidly, they do the same. — Jacqui Canney, ServiceNow.

Recent findings suggest that if you want real accountability, let team members own the outcome and cut the endless approval chains. Nobody likes to fail, but you can build a culture of permissible failure and actually walk the talk. When mistakes happen, address them head-on, take the lesson, and move on fast. — Khozema Shipchandler, Twilio.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss.
  • Bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter.
  • Sources indicate that the pace stands out against the wider market.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss. The online unit still lost money, and the results came with another delayed quarterly filing after a going-concern warning in August.

Bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter. It is still not profitable. North America Interactive groups the firm’s sports betting and iGaming businesses in both countries. The unit lost less money than a year earlier, but it stayed in the red.

Sources indicate that the pace stands out against the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, according to Citizens JMP Securities. That was down from 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. Bally’s online growth ran well ahead of that slowing trend.

In a recent development, the quarter was not a clean step up, though. North America Interactive posted $66.1 million in second-quarter revenue, up 16.9% from a year earlier. Third-quarter sales were therefore lower than the quarter before. First-quarter revenue was $60.5 million, a 35.9% increase.

Industry observers note that for the first nine months of 2026, the unit had preliminary revenue of $189.2 million. That compares with $134.0 million for February 8 to September 30, 2025, and $16.9 million for January 1 to February 7, 2025.

In a recent development, A narrower loss points to progress. Yet the unit has not reached break-even, even while growing faster than the market. For a smaller US operator, online scale is still not translating into profit.

In a recent development, all third-quarter figures are preliminary. Bally’s has not finished closing its books for the period ended September 30, 2026, and the numbers could change. It filed a late-filing notice dated November 10 because it needed more time to finish reviewing its third-quarter financial statements.

That makes three late quarterly reports in 2026. Bally’s notified the SEC in May that its first-quarter report would be late. It did the same in August for the second quarter. Both notices cited more time needed to review financial statements.

Industry observers note that in the first-quarter 10-Q, management concluded that disclosure controls were not effective. The cause was a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting, first disclosed in the 2025 annual report.

In a recent development, the second-quarter 10-Q, filed August 14, went further. Two tests tied to the firm’s revolver, a net leverage covenant and a liquidity requirement, were expected to be missed during the coming year. That same filing carried a going-concern warning, questioning whether Bally’s could keep operating. The shares fell more than 25% in one trading session afterward.

In a recent development, bally’s reports strong revenue growth in Q3 2026. Data and info: https://t.co/ekSd5Ngu0Q.

• Group revenue increased 22% to USD 807.6m, while North America Interactive revenue rose 26% to USD 62.7m.

— OGQ-Magazine (Online Gambling Quarterly) (@OGQMagazine) November 10, 2026.

Industry observers note that CEO Robeson Reeves noted development projects remain on track and market conditions are stable going into the fourth quarter and 2027. The Bronx casino resort is expected to cost $4.0 billion and open by 2030. Bally’s closed a financing package led by WhiteHawk Capital Partners that provided $400 million in term loans for the project. Another $160 million in delayed-draw commitments remains available. The term loans come due 18 months after they are first funded.

Recent findings suggest that the delayed third-quarter 10-Q comes next. The organization has said it should arrive before its five-day SEC grace period runs out.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

It has been revealed that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

The direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:.

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

Sources indicate that the first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

The second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:.

It has been revealed that on a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a new connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

Industry observers note that A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a newly introduced connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

Node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for new connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:.

Second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:.

It has been revealed that we then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

This advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

For each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

Industry observers note that the interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:.

In a recent development, an interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:.

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:.

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

Industry observers note that liteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point indicates up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

According to recent reports, logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

If 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

Before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that researchers have used reinforcement learning to teach a 5-tonne John Deere skid-steer loader to perform complex acrobatic manoeuvres autonomously.
  • If you unfurl the video embed above, you can see a hulking 332G skid-steer do some astonishing tricks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that videos of an incredibly acrobatic, nimble, and graceful John Deere 5-ton skid-steer loader have been shared by a group of researchers from the U.S. and Switzerland. A recently published paper titled Heavy Metal Acrobatics provides the reasoning behind this eyebrow-raising autonomous robotics feat. It is hoped this research will be useful in the future automation of heavy machinery in industries like construction, mining, and material handling. It also demonstrates that reinforcement learning in a simulation can transfer remarkably well to the real world.

Industry observers note that researchers have used reinforcement learning to teach a 5-tonne John Deere skid-steer loader to perform complex acrobatic manoeuvres autonomously. Trained in simulation and transferred to a real machine, the system can balance on two wheels, navigate rough terrain, spin, and control its bucket before landing safely. The research demonstrates the potential of AI-driven automation for heavy construction and industrial machinery. Video Credit: @leggedrobotics / @ETH Paper: https://t.co/MT7fyZ54Hk #engineering #technologyNovember 17, 2026.

If you unfurl the video embed above, you can see a hulking 332G skid-steer do some astonishing tricks. It hops back and forth on two wheels, pirouettes, and balances while flexing its lift arm. Moreover, it does these moves while never looking like it will teeter over. The researchers claim that “only a handful of elite human operators” have ever been able to pull off stunts as you see in the demo videos.

The technology behind the remarkable acrobatic skid-steer is mostly Reinforcement Learning (RL), with physics modeling and neural network models. As machinery like this is so big, powerful, and bulky, undertaking RL directly on the hardware wasn’t deemed practical. Instead, the research team decided to use a simulation programmed with the John Deere 332G’s complex array of controls for training. This data was subsequently applied to the actual skid-steer via a sim-to-real transfer. The simulations must be extremely accurate.

This acrobatic goliath is impressive, but of course there’s an underlying goal driving Heavy Metal Acrobatics’ research. The scientists are laying the foundations for the enabling of “dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery.” It is hoped this will help promote greater automation in heavy equipment sectors of industry. Eventually, autonomous control should be safer, faster, and more efficient than any human.

Recent findings suggest that with these video demonstrations of nimble and highly maneuverable heavy machinery, it is clear that there’s more scope for AI-driven automation than one may have previously expected. Furthermore, it looks like being a skilled heavy machinery operator is definitely not an AI-proof occupation.

#23962. Anthropic stock is already falling today: Why AI giants are seeing a painful sell-off after record IPO

Anthropic stock is already falling today: Why AI giants are seeing a painful sell-off after record IPO

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks.
  • Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks.
  • Nearly every major hardware manufacturer that makes components for the AI pipeline—from CPUs to GPUs to memory—is seeing significant share price declines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks. And today things are even worse. Nearly every major hardware manufacturer that makes components for the AI pipeline—from CPUs to GPUs to memory—is seeing significant share price declines. And then there’s Anthropic itself, the world’s most valuable pure-play AI company. After a strong debut yesterday, its share price is down significantly this morning. Here’s what you need to know. What’s happening? In premarket trading this morning, the tech-heavy Nasdaq is seeing red, along with some of the largest AI players that trade there. As of this writing, Nasdaq futures are down nearly 1%. That’s after a significant fall of more than 550 points, or 2.25% yesterday. As of Thursday’s close, the Nasdaq was down around 5% for the week. Yesterday’s Nasdaq drop is all the more striking because it was also the day that Anthropic made its eagerly awaited market debut. The AI company’s IPO was priced at $83 per share, but those shares rapidly popped to nearly $115 in early trading before ending the first day at $97.17—a 17% gain. Anthropic’s IPO was the largest in history, raising around $81.3 billion. The company’s market cap now sits at around $1.27 billion, making it the 12th most valuable company on the planet. Yet Anthropic’s success did little for the rest of the market. Throughout the day, tech stocks started falling, including those of other major AI players like Nvidia. This morning, Asian markets and major AI and tech players are down significantly. And on this side of the Pacific, the sell-off is continuing with major American AI-related stocks. As of the time of this writing, the following AI-adjacent stocks are down in premarket:  Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMD): down 6.5% NVIDIA Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA): down 2.3% Intel Corporation (Nasdaq: INTC): down 5.2% Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU): down 4.8% SanDisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK): down 6.7% And yes, Anthropic’s stock price is down nearly 10%. Why are Anthropic’s shares sinking? Anthropic and hardware-related AI companies are both seeing their share prices sink in premarket trading, but maybe for different reasons. When it comes to AI hardware companies, those that make the components needed to power the massive server farms AI data centers require, there has been significant negative sentiment around them since at least October. Investors are increasingly getting uneasy with the major hyperscalers’ capex spending. Companies like Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions to build out data centers, and most aren’t yet showing a clear path to monetizing AI enough to recoup those costs. If those companies cave to investor pressure and start scaling back their capex plans, it will hit AI hardware component makers (like Nvidia, Intel, and AMD) and memory makers (like Micron and SanDisk) pretty hard. Investors seem to be bracing for an inevitable capex pullback, which has weighed heavily on hardware-adjacent AI stocks recently. Other factors that have affected AI stocks lately include the Jensen Huang scandal and the ongoing fears that we are firmly in an AI bubble. But Anthropic doesn’t make hardware, and it just had its successful IPO only yesterday—so why are its shares down so much today? It likely has less to do with significant fears of capex spending and more to do with other factors. The primary factor is likely profit-taking. The company’s stock price rose more than 17% on its first day of trading. Many shareholders who aren’t bound by lockup periods are likely taking some of those profits this morning. Another factor—and one that could have significantly more long-term consequences—is that fears of an AI bubble and an AI slowdown are also likely weighing on investors’ minds. Anthropic has a massive valuation north of $1.2 trillion, but in the first nine months of 2026, the company generated only around $33 billion in revenue. Its net loss for the same period was $104 billion. Investors may be able to live with that discrepancy while the AI hype train is riding high, but enthusiasm only goes so far, and if the AI bubble bursts, Anthropic could be hit hard. Where do Anthropic shares go from here? That’s something everyone wants to know, and no one can tell you. The company’s share price has already fallen from its intraday debut high of nearly $115 per share to its current premarket price of $88.44. Contrast that with the company Anthropic just dethroned as having the largest IPO in history: SpaceX. When SpaceX (Nasdaq: SPCX) went public in June, it was, until yesterday, the biggest IPO in history, raising $75 billion. Its IPO price was $135 per share, and the stock quickly jumped to more than $225 per share. But then it began falling. A month after its debut, SPCX shares were trading below their $135 IPO price as the hype wore off, and people began questioning the company’s future profitability. As of the time of this writing, SPCX shares are trading at just $131.66 in premarket trading. If ANT’s early life plays out the same way—and there’s no way to predict whether it will or won’t—the share price could be underwater for even IPO investors in just a few months. And if the AI bubble does burst, things could get even worse.

Latest Update: MotorCity Casino Gains 15.6% as MGM and Greektown Slip in Detroit’s October Revenue

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Growth at MotorCity Casino outweighed declines at MGM Grand Detroit and Hollywood Casino at Greektown, lifting Detroit's October table and slot revenue from a year earlier.
  • MotorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier.
  • Industry observers note that across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Growth at MotorCity Casino outweighed declines at MGM Grand Detroit and Hollywood Casino at Greektown, lifting Detroit's October table and slot revenue from a year earlier. Retail sports betting also rebounded sharply from September, adding to the month's gains.

MotorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier. Its rivals both lost ground. MGM Grand Detroit slipped 2.7% to $51.3 million. Hollywood Casino at Greektown fell 5.0% to $21.6 million.

Industry observers note that across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million. That was up 2.1% from October 2025 and 5.2% from September 2026. Year-to-date revenue from January through October was up 2.3%.

CDC Gaming Reports put October 2025 table and slot revenue at $105.9 million.

In a recent development, MGM still holds the largest piece of the market. It took 47% of Detroit’s October revenue. MotorCity held 33%, and Hollywood Casino at Greektown held 20%.

The October split continues a pattern from late summer. In August, MotorCity rose 8.3% to $33.8 million and MGM grew 2.3% to $52.9 million, while Greektown fell 2.6% to $22.2 million, InterGame reported. Detroit’s August total was $109.7 million.

Greektown’s slide deepened in September, when its revenue fell 8.8% year over year to $21.34 million. October’s decline was smaller. MGM, by contrast, moved from growth in August to a decline in October.

In a recent development, the citywide trend has been uneven. September table and slot revenue was 4.7% higher than a year earlier but 5.6% lower than in August. October’s rebound lifted aggregate revenue above September’s $103.55 million.

According to recent reports, retail sports betting produced $2.4 million in October. That compares with $769,771 in retail QAGR in September. Handle at the Detroit casinos was $12.87 million for the month.

In a recent development, motorCity also led the sportsbook results. It posted $928,607 in retail receipts. MGM followed at $746,215, with Hollywood Casino at Greektown close behind at $729,350.

The sportsbook activity generated $90,878 in state taxes. The casinos also sent $111,073 in sports wagering taxes to Detroit.

According to recent reports, the city’s take from the casinos goes well beyond sports betting. In October, Detroit collected $13.4 million from the three properties, combining its share of gaming taxes with sums owed under each casino’s agreement with the city.

In a recent development, A grand total of $9,985,482+ in jackpots hit at MotorCity Casino in October! 💰🎰.

Congratulations to all the guests who took home a win! Here’s to an exciting November! pic.twitter.com/bHIJGmc0jM.

— MotorCity Casino (@MotorCityCasino) November 8, 2026.

Fantasy contests remain a small part of the picture. Operators reported $837,938 in adjusted revenues for September 2026 and paid $70,387 in taxes.

Detroit’s land-based results now set a baseline for Michigan’s October online casino and sports betting figures, which come next. In September, the state’s commercial and tribal online operators took in $355.7 million in combined iGaming and online sports betting gross receipts, 5.4% more than in August.

#23960. Texas Democrats’ sweeping victory could spell trouble for Elon Musk’s business empire

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2360 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Texas Democrats’ sweeping victory could spell trouble for Elon Musk’s business empire

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets.
  • Hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets.
  • “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” the world’s richest man stated at The Newly introduced York Times DealBook conference this week, reflecting on the heaps of dollars he poured into Republican campaigns nationwide during this year’s midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets. “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” the world’s richest man noted at The Newly introduced York Times DealBook conference this week, reflecting on the heaps of dollars he poured into Republican campaigns nationwide during this year’s midterm elections. It’s easy to see why he feels that way, particularly in Texas, where Musk has moved his business operations and cultivated close ties with Republican leadership. Despite his extraordinary spending—$446 million, roughly half of which went to races in Texas—Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress and swept the major statewide elections. That eye-popping figure includes $5 million for Republican incumbent Greg Abbott’s gubernatorial campaign and $10 million for Attorney General Ken Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid, both of which ended in defeat. But Musk may soon have much bigger financial headaches than any futile campaign contributions. The incoming Democratic administration in Austin could complicate the billionaire’s aims to expand his sprawling business empire. Indeed, Texas’s governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, has already signaled that she intends to be less accommodating of the kinds of tax breaks and land deals that helped lure Musk to the Lone Star State in the first place. Abbott has by contrast been an enthusiastic champion of Musk’s Texas vision, appearing alongside him at organization events and celebrating his investments in the state. Abbott and Musk reportedly keep in close contact, and the governor’s office even fought to prevent the release of months of communications with the tech mogul’s companies, arguing that they contain “information that is intimate and embarrassing and not of legitimate concern to the public.” With Hinojosa in office, Musk can no longer count on that same level of intimacy, though he did offer a more sanguine assessment of his future in a blue Texas at the DealBook conference, predicting that Hinojosa would govern as a moderate. “I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said. Billions in tax breaks Musk’s companies have to date been given the royal treatment from the state. SpaceX, for instance, scored roughly $1.66 billion in potential property tax breaks for its planned Terafab semiconductor facility in Grimes County, between College Station and Houston, according to the Houston Chronicle. The incentives, approved by two local school districts under Texas’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation program, could cut the company’s school property taxes in half for 10 years per phase of construction. SpaceX also secured a $30 million grant from the Texas Enterprise Fund. Hinojosa has made no secret of her disdain for such arrangements. “I do think we should wipe clean corporate welfare in this state,” she told the Texas Standard in October, singling out Musk’s billion-dollar-plus tax break. She’s also pushing to reveal to the public more about Musk’s relationship with Abbott. In October, she sued Abbott for access to unredacted emails involving Musk and his companies. But Hinojosa won’t have an easy time undoing those incentives. She would have considerable discretion over the Texas Enterprise Fund, although recovering money already awarded would depend on the grant’s terms. Reversing the much larger property tax breaks would prove far more difficult. Those agreements are made among the company, local school districts, and the governor, who cannot simply terminate them over a change in policy. State law does allow the governor to revoke the incentives if a company fails to meet certain employment or wage requirements, but even then, the company must be given an opportunity to remedy or challenge the violation. To that end, Hinojosa has said she plans on reviewing Musk’s existing incentives to ensure his companies are meeting employment obligations. Those requirements can be remarkably lenient: Per the Chronicle, SpaceX needs to create just 80 jobs at its Terafab facility to meet the minimum employment threshold for the school-district tax incentives. SpaceX’s South Texas expansion Hinojosa’s victory could also throw a wrench into SpaceX’s expansion plans in South Texas, where the company is pursuing massive new infrastructure projects—and seeking additional land for its operations. For starters, there’s the $24 billion data center and natural gas-fired power plant planned near its Starbase headquarters near the border with Mexico. SpaceX confirmed the project earlier this month and claims construction activity has already created more than 3,000 jobs, though the facility is not yet operational. (That project has already encountered resistance from local officials, with Cameron County commissioners voting this week 3–2 against advancing SpaceX’s request for a 10-year, 100% property-tax abatement for the project.) Hinojosa has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center approvals until Texas lawmakers enact stronger protections for water supplies, electricity customers, and surrounding communities. And she’s also indicated that projects already underway wouldn’t necessarily be exempt: “If it needs a permit that the state has to approve, then that’s on hold,” she told the Chronicle last week. Again, though, SpaceX has gotten a head start. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality this week approved an air permit for a natural gas plant associated with the project. But that permit covers only the power-generating component, not the entire $24 billion development. So Hinojosa could still hold up the project if SpaceX needs additional state approvals once she takes office. Meanwhile, SpaceX has also been pursuing a deal to acquire state-owned parkland near its Boca Chica launch facility, at the mouth of the Rio Grande. Texas Monthly reported last month that state officials were considering selling 1,300 acres to the company, raising obvious questions around coastal access and habitat preservation. Hinojosa, who grew up in nearby Brownsville, asked the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department shortly after her election to hold off on any action during the transition. SpaceX has since clarified that it wants approximately 1,200 acres of public parkland surrounding its launch facility—not Boca Chica Beach itself—and says it would preserve half the property as coastal habitat. And SpaceX could face another headache at Boca Chica. Benjamin Flores, the Democrat who is the incoming Texas land commissioner, plans to challenge a 2013 law allowing temporary beach closures for rocket releases, Texas Monthly reports. And while the state Supreme Court threw out a previous challenge in June, that rejection came on procedural grounds, leaving the law’s constitutionality unresolved. A possible Tesla–SpaceX merger Tesla and SpaceX have been discussing a merger, which would bring Musk’s EV, rocket, satellite and AI businesses under one corporate roof. The state’s new Democratic leadership could throw a wrench into those plans. Texas’s incoming attorney general, Nathan Johnson, has already signaled that he intends to take a very close look at any such tie-up. “Any merger of companies of that consequence warrants tremendous scrutiny,” he told Bloomberg last week, citing concerns about corporate concentration. Johnson’s office could investigate potential antitrust violations and, if deemed warranted, challenge the merger in court. Unlike Hinojosa’s proposed data center restrictions, which could require new legislation or regulations, that authority already exists under state law.|.

Hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” the world’s richest man stated at The Newly introduced York Times DealBook conference this week, reflecting on the heaps of dollars he poured into Republican campaigns nationwide during this year’s midterm elections.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions. Signal is the latest platform to make changes. The encrypted messaging app is preventing screenshots on any device with Apple’s iOS 27 in a bid to stop AI agents from accessing sensitive information. It will also block AI assistants from capturing screen data on Android devices. “An existential threat’ Meredith Whittaker, president of Signal Technology Foundation, the nonprofit that runs the Signal app, revealed the change in a blog post. Whittaker pointed to how Google, Apple, and Microsoft’s “agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.” The app can now block Siri AI and turn on “screen security” as a means of preventing AI assistants from scanning information. Users can turn off the protections, but Signal warns that this could leave messages exposed and remove the app’s privacy guarantee. Signal took similar measures last year on Windows 11 to protect messages from Microsoft Recall, a feature that periodically captures and stores screenshots of your work. Signal is fed up with a lack of AI assistant transparency The current blog post seeps with frustration at Signal’s inability to do more to protect privacy amid a lack of transparency from tech giants. “We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal—and application developers beyond—lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” states Whittaker. She explained that Signal has struggled due to limited information about how any of these AI agents work, being forced to do its own forensic investigations into how the “AI systems access application data.”  The blog post calls on makers of major operating systems to provide tools and information about how the AI agents work and how they can be prevented from accessing sensitive data. She further stated that apps should have a way to opt out of AI tools like screen reading without having to compromise their core utility. Whittaker problems a clear warning: “Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.”.

Industry News: OpenAI's AI models boost AMD's upcoming flagship GPU design by up to 14% in PPA

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, openAI just revealed newly introduced details about its ongoing partnership with AMD, in which engineers used undisclosed AI models to help optimize the hardware maker's upcoming flagship GPU and CPU designs.
  • Sources indicate that openAI states that its model spotted "further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits." This work was done in SystemVerilog RTL, the language commonly used for high-end chip design.
  • Furthermore, OpenAI says its model was reasoning on RTL "at the level of an expert microarchitect," and that it expects to squeeze further PPA improvements in both GPU and CPU designs, up from the now-improved baseline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openAI just revealed newly introduced details about its ongoing partnership with AMD, in which engineers used undisclosed AI models to help optimize the hardware maker's upcoming flagship GPU and CPU designs. The leading figures are up to 14% PPA (power, performance, and area) improvement for the GPU circuitry, and unspecified single-digit PPA gains on the processor.

Sources indicate that openAI states that its model spotted "further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits." This work was done in SystemVerilog RTL, the language commonly used for high-end chip design. The firm claims that its model's optimization efforts are equivalent to condensing a year's worth of conventional chip design work into "under 5 months" — a time crunch it says is unprecedented in this arena.

Furthermore, OpenAI says its model was reasoning on RTL "at the level of an expert microarchitect," and that it expects to squeeze further PPA improvements in both GPU and CPU designs, up from the now-improved baseline.

Industry observers note that this isn't AI's first time working on chips. It worked with Broadcom on designing OpenAI Jalapeño, an inference-targeted chip that was already running actual workloads with engineering samples as far back as June 2026.

The company expected to have small initial Jalapeño deployments around late 2026, and pinned a broader rollout to 2027. Test benchmarks have been out for a while, displaying purported excellent savings on power draw and overall latency versus the market-leading Nvidia Blackwell GPUs in single-token prediction workloads.

The blog post also explains how GPT's chip-design acumen evolved. The researchers tested its high-end LLMs by asking them to improve PicoRV32 and Ibex chip cores. The models were given 112,000 tokens per run, told to optimize for throughput (a combination of Instructions-per-Clock and clock-cycle duration), and scored the results.

A fat zero was given if the chips didn't work or used more than 16x the previous area, and 1.0 was given for the best designs under the test constraints. The test also didn't tell the models which workloads the chips were going to be used for. As expected, GPT-6.2 Astra had by far the best showing, on both axes: both the lowest overall cost and the highest optimization score.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

A second test also revealed an interesting but unsurprising fact: the models provided better results when essentially redesigning the chips according to their initial specifications, rather than optimizing existing code.

Recent findings suggest that there's no word on whether the scientists used unmodified versions of GPT to perform this work. Task-specific high-end LLMs exist for those who can afford them, and OpenAI itself indicates it's working with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsis, a model for using chip design tools.

How Thanksgiving travelers are feeling about holiday air travel after widespread tech outages

  • In a recent development, at this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.And for 2026’s busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there’s another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, at this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.And for 2026’s busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there’s another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She’s pretty sure she’s not the only one.“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having … I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” stated Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.It’s an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days’ tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it’s a familiar one, too.Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it’s one they’re likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.” Air travel is vital — and taken for granted In some ways, the country’s aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy … and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.“You’ve got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There’s nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she’s used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she’s not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she’s not rattled by it.“I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami.She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.”And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to “Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something,” she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?” The expense can be as much of an obstacle as the delays If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can’t just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter’s flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.She saw a promotion on American Airlines’ online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it’s a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn’t go bad. She’s keeping the rolls in her garage“The funny part,” she said, “is we have to buy toilet paper anyway.” AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story. —Deepti Hajela, Associated Press.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A Redditor from the UK was flying from the United States with their desktop PC in a carry-on but was forced to check it. According to u/FattyLeopold, they’ve carried their PC as a carry-on on different flights, and they brought it with them in the cabin all the way across the Atlantic. The trip even included a layover.

In a recent development, “It was 4am, and I was pissed off,” the Redditor replied to one comment. “Just said fu-- it, let’s see what happens. Probably confused the universe a bit, ‘Dude… what are you doing… Aight, have it your way.’” They then taped the PC, monitor, and keyboard together in the package.

Recent findings suggest that the desktop PC only had a bag and several layers of protective wrapping for protection. What’s more surprising is that the owner didn’t even take the GPU off its bracket and put it in their carry-on. When they arrived at their destination, they recorded the “unboxing” of their PC. Against all odds, their computer arrived without a single dent or scratch — the tempered glass on the side of the PC didn’t even shatter after the possible trauma it went through in baggage handling.

Most of us have seen videos of airport baggage handlers throwing bags and packages around while they’re loading them onto the plane, not to mention the bumps and tumbles that luggage takes when going through an airport’s baggage conveyor system. The PC also has to deal with the vibration and turbulence of flight. The shortest direct flight across the pond is about 6 hours and 30 minutes — since the Redditor said that they had a layover, that meant that the desktop PC had been in transit for a bit longer than that.

Industry observers note that it’s a miracle that the computer was able to make it through the journey without a scratch, but the Redditor is not out of the woods yet. They mentioned that even though the computer looked undamaged on the surface, they haven’t been able to boot it yet because they do not have a proper adapter for outlets in the UK. Hopefully, they could get it working after finding the right plug or adapter for their computer, or with some basic troubleshooting (like re-plugging the components) if it won’t turn on after the first try. GPUs and memory sticks are quite expensive these days, after all, and it’s unlikely that AMD would replace their graphics card because of this misadventure, unlike this $10,000 RTX Pro 6000 that Nvidia replaced after a customer who bought it new broke the GPU in transit.

Sources indicate that this year’s U.N. climate talks are wrapping up in Turkey, with negotiators fighting over how to address global warming and experts warning that only slashing fossil fuels can avert its most catastrophic effects.Activists and country leaders were in an uproar Friday, the last scheduled day of the two-week summit known as COP31, after the term “fossil fuels” was left out of the final agreement’s draft.Climate summits often end with a final text, meant to address how the world will deal with climate change. Such agreements — often adopted by nearly 200 nations — are still voluntary and non-binding.Negotiators, who pulled an all-nighter from Thursday into Friday, noted they expect COP31 to go into overtime on Saturday. Worries about a ‘worst COP ever’ Past COPs have failed to agree on how to transition away from fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas — that warm the planet, heat the oceans and worsen air quality. Climate change also intensified several of this year’s disasters, like Europe’s deadly heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding.If fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement, this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa.In a rare move, Panama vowed to “formally object” if the final agreement doesn’t add climate finance, cap oil production, and acknowledge failing goals, among other demands. The country’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks are being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and need to be reformed.“The COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility,” he said. “What we have here is a contest to see who speaks the most, who blows the most hot air.”In the lead up to COP31, the United Nations announced the world is dangerously close to missing its decades-old goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.“There is nothing on the table that protects people, or addresses the priorities of the Global South,” said Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, at a Friday event, where attendees chanted and held signs that read “SHAME!” As climate talks near their end, fossil fuel debate rages One of the main deals on the table at COP31 is an electrification goal to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.But the final draft doesn’t spell out that this should be reached with renewable energy sources, like solar and wind — leaving the door open for fossil fuel power plants to be counted as part of an electrification push.“At a time when the climate crisis demands decisive action, weakening commitments on fossil fuel phase-out risks undermining progress,” said Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace in the Middle East and North Africa.The U.N. has hosted climate talks for more than 30 years but it was only in 2021 during COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, that nations first acknowledged fossil fuels contribute to climate change.Two years later during COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, countries explicitly called for a transition away from fossil fuels for the first time.Turkey and Australia, co-hosts of COP31, are being roundly criticized for removing fossil fuels from the final text’s draft.“We are not here to discuss decisions at previous COPs,” said Turkey’s Minister of Environment Murat Kurum, who is overseeing the summit held in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. The electrification push implies a transition away from fossil fuels, he said.“Removing those words from a document will not remove the pollution from the atmosphere,” said Adow of Power Shift Africa. “It simply exposes how far these negotiations have become detached from what is needed outside this conference center.” Vulnerable nations say climate finance is lacking Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable nations that don’t emit a lot of greenhouse gases — have said that rich countries are not providing previously agreed upon funds to deal with climate change.They said that U.N. funds for adapting to climate risks, dealing with climate impacts and funds for clean energy infrastructure don’t match what the U.N. has said these countries need.The draft agreement states the need to triple the amount of money for countries adapting to climate impacts, but it doesn’t specify how much. One of the draft’s previous versions stated at least $120 billion would be needed annually.Many of the world’s most polluting nations did not participate directly at this year’s talks, including the United States, the world’s largest economy and a major emitter.It’s richer nations, like the U.S., that vulnerable countries want funding from — and it’s hard to ask for funds without American officials in the room.Efforts to slow global warming have essentially stalled for the past five years, according to a recent report by the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker.“Disappointment is rife,” said Iskander Erzini Vernoit, an adviser to African negotiators in Turkey. Next year’s climate summit is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.“Hope is not lost, but absent a course correction, we are headed toward a low-ambition set of outcomes at COP31,” he said. Associated Press writer Tammy Webber contributed to this report. The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as everyday technology becomes more advanced, parents are prioritizing screen-free, hands-on holiday gifts for children. Forty-one percent of people buying gifts for kids in their family are leaning toward screen-free gifts, according to a survey by PwC. A Germany-based brand called Tonies created an interactive, screen-free audio player designed for children. The most well-known toy, called the Toniebox, is a squishy, cube-shaped speaker controlled completely by the child. Some models come with a hand-painted, magnetic figurine that automatically plays audiobooks, songs, or stories when placed on the box. Last holiday season, the Tonies app hit No. 1 on the App Store. This year, the company saw a 33% increase in global revenue in the first nine months of 2026. Its biggest market is North America, capturing $315 million in revenue in 2025. Concerns about screen use in childhood Screen use in early years of childhood has shown potential to harm cognitive, linguistic, and social-emotional growth, according to a study from the National Library of Medicine. Excessive screen use among youth has even been linked to a rise in likelihood of obesity, sleep disorders, and depression, and anxiety, the study found. Screens have the potential to improve education and learning, when paired with parental controls and screen-time restrictions. But, Tonies offers a chance for children to interact with their minds rather than a touch-screen. “Through listening, the key thing is, your imagination develops because you actually picture the dragon, you picture the knight, you picture whatever it is. It’s not just delivered for you,” Mark McColgan, general manager, North America at Tonies, told Fast Company. The company started producing the Toniebox 10 years ago. The company started producing the Toniebox 10 years ago, and while new versions are released, the boxes are built for long-term use, stated McColgan, who joined Tonies this year from Mattel. The boxes are a relief for busy parents, too. Sometimes parents need a moment to themselves, but offering a screen to their children for a short-term distraction can become a long-term addiction, and a source of guilt for parents. Some parents have turned to screens to curb behavior in public, and sometimes, as a replacement for expensive childcare, a study from a hospital found. “It gives them guilt-free time to do something else, because when their child is playing with the Toniebox, they know it’s a safe, good environment for them to do so,” McColgan said. This story was updated to clarify that new versions of the Toniebox have been released since the product launched.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what do you keep in your emergency bag? The one for when the electrical grid goes down. Or all the banks stop working. Or the world is ending. First aid essentials. N95 masks. A pocket-size book of human anatomy. Solar-powered chargers and small knives. A compass and a road atlas of the continental U.S. That’s what Gina Arconti keeps in her Béis Weekender bag in case of emergencies. “Something some people don’t know about me is I’m a little bit of a doomsday prepper,” she stated in a recent TikTok video, now with over 400,000 views. The video was posted last week, after Microsoft Outlook went down. Then flights across the U.S. were grounded. Then Apple Pay stopped working. On Tuesday, the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network temporarily went down. You don’t have to be a conspiracy theorist to wonder what’s going on. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday that “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” But for longtime doomsday preppers, the writing is on the wall. “Amazon doomsday haul,” Jeff For, another TikTok user based in Los Angeles, said in a video posted earlier this month. His purchases include a hand-crank portable radio that doubles as a flashlight, phone charger, compass, and SOS signal. He also bought a collapsible water jug, candles, and a mini drone. “If I’m stuck or I don’t want to leave where I am I can use this bad boy to fly up in the air and see everything around me,” he explains. Some are rushing to stock up on supplies from Costco or $395 emergency backpacks containing everything from a pop-up tube tent to dried ice cream. Others have been squirreling away supplies for years, preparing for this exact moment. Online preppers are also seeing a surge of views amid the outages. “So you just started your prepping journey and you’re not really sure what the next step will be,” said Krystal, known online as the “Doomsday Queen,” to her 132,000 Instagram followers earlier this month. The video’s caption directs viewers to her free Beginner’s Preparedness Guide. View this post on Instagram Others preach off-grid self-sufficiency, offering tutorials on food storage, emergency water supplies, and what to do when the toilets no longer flush. But some may be overlooking the first rule of doomsday prep: Don’t tell anyone about your doomsday prep. Otherwise, where do you think everyone will head when the world actually ends?

#23951. The Nvidia CEO scandal is impacting Asian American women in tech and academia. Here’s how

📖 Baca
